title: Decision models for Pac-Man — Kev, CLM and the lab

slides.title: Kev and CLM
slides.body: Our lab follows Kev's LoRA + pointer-head recipe.
slides.footer: Pac-Man lab | 90 minutes | 30-minute fine-tuning block
slides.notes:
Small-model Kev trains low-rank encoder adapters and a pointer head. Original base matrices stay fixed, but effective features change. CLM trains state/action projection heads and a similarity scale over completely fixed LLM features. Kev-27B is a separate full-fine-tuning recipe. The Pac-Man lab uses Kev-0.8B with the published decision-v7 base stage, then supervised player-domain adaptation. The comparison remains useful for understanding independent action caching and repeated training cost.
Sources: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/84847f0a883d900f7de5b7a57eaa341ca7f9a6b4/kev/model.py ; https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM/blob/bb42c6c5bf914fd449bed2f6ca65be80602cb1f7/src/clm/heads.py ; supplied Contrastive Language Models PDF pages 6-8.

slides.body: Accuracy depends on the backbone, data and task.
slides.footer: Architectural tradeoffs; neither approach is always better
slides.notes:
Kev's joint causal representation can model state/option interactions before its readout. LoRA can adapt those representations but its benefit over a head-only variant requires a controlled ablation. CLM's independent encodings support reusable actions and cached backbone features; its learned heads can remap existing features but cannot guarantee recovery of information absent from the frozen representation. A larger CLM backbone can offset some representation limitations; this is an architectural inference, not a measured accuracy ordering.
Sources: pinned Kev model.py; pinned CLM heads.py and train/finetune.py; supplied CLM PDF pages 6-8.

slides.body: Compare total cost: feature extraction + all training runs.
slides.footer: CLM's reported ~1-hour run assumes precomputed embeddings
slides.notes:
Conceptual accounting, not dollar estimates: CLM total work = feature extraction + the sum of head-training runs; Kev LoRA = the sum of encoder forward/backward plus head/adapter training runs. A feature cache can be reused across random seeds and head settings while backbone, tokenizer, pooling and input recipe stay fixed. The CLM PDF reports about one hour on an RTX 4090 for the Nemotron head pretraining run after describing precomputed LLM embeddings. It does not establish the end-to-end time including extraction, download, dataset preparation or synthetic-negative generation. A LoRA model has fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning but still needs encoder activations and backpropagation. Free quotas change payments, not the amount of compute. Record actual hardware-hours rather than inventing prices.
Sources: supplied CLM PDF page 6; https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM/blob/bb42c6c5bf914fd449bed2f6ca65be80602cb1f7/train/finetune.py ; pinned Kev model.py and train.py.

slides.body: *Parameter count × 2 bytes; excludes heads, cache and runtime.
slides.footer: Raw weight arithmetic is not a measured VRAM requirement
slides.notes:
Decimal GB estimates use rounded parameter counts and BF16's two bytes per parameter. They exclude tokenizer/embedding peculiarities, heads, KV or recurrent state, activations, quantization metadata and runtime overhead. Do not present these as peak memory measurements. CLM's state and action paths can use one shared frozen backbone instance. CLM action reuse saves repeated action token encoding; it is especially useful with repeated or many/long actions. It does not guarantee that released CLM-8B beats released Kev-0.8B or Kev-4B on four short directions. Quantization and backend implementations also affect serving cost and accuracy.
Sources: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev ; https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM ; supplied CLM PDF pages 6-8.

slides.body: These reports do not establish a Kev-versus-CLM speed ranking.
slides.footer: Different hardware and workloads; use a paired lab benchmark
slides.notes:
CLM PDF page 7: a 200-token state, 15 tokens per candidate, one RTX 4090 and five trials; latency rises from 36 ms for one cached candidate to 44 ms for 1,024. Its ~13x at 1,024 candidates is versus hosted Jev, not Kev. The llama.cpp announcement reports a 12 ms median for Kev-4B on RTX PRO 6000 for one question; it is not a matched run against CLM. Never divide 36 by 12 to infer a comparative speedup. No matched Kev-vs-CLM Pac-Man benchmark was identified in the reviewed sources. Their published accuracy suites and training data differ. Our 16-board sample is only a demonstration, not evidence of general superiority.
Sources: supplied CLM PDF page 7; https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/decision-models-in-llamacpp ; https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev ; https://github.com/Contrastive-LM/CLM .

slides.body: CLM is outside this release's five supported models.
slides.footer: Julia, Laya, Kev and lev: Apache 2.0 | OpenJev: CC BY-NC 4.0
slides.notes:
Supported list is the October 2, 2026 release, not an exhaustive list of decision models. Julia and Laya use the same laya-style backend in llama.cpp: ModernBERT-family encoder, two decision transformer layers, type embedding and per-option MASK-marker scorer. Julia's training pipeline and exact freezing policy are not disclosed. Laya's published root architecture fully fine-tunes ModernBERT-large. Kev's small-model recipe trains LoRA and a pointer head. lev conversion supports mode A vocabulary-label readout only, not its mode B candidate-path head. Choice is evaluated in two orders and averaged. OpenJev is an independent project, not TypeSafe's hosted Jev; its card specifies decision tuning but not exactly which components received gradients. OpenJev's llama.cpp build supports a multimodal projector, even though some earlier quantized builds in its author's card are text-only. Do not generalize multilingual Laya subfolder capabilities to the English root checkpoint.
Sources: https://huggingface.co/blog/ggml-org/decision-models-in-llamacpp ; https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29818 ; https://huggingface.co/SupersonicLabs/Julia-1 ; https://huggingface.co/convaiinnovations/laya ; https://huggingface.co/interfaze-ai/lev ; https://huggingface.co/openjev/openjev .

slides.title: How llama.cpp scores decisions
slides.body:
POST /v1/systemone: Choice, Score and Noul
GGUF metadata selects the model's readout
Kev's LoRA is merged before quantization
No generated answer tokens to parse
CLM needs its own serving implementation
slides.footer: API compatibility does not mean architectural equivalence
slides.notes:
The merged llama.cpp PR adds decision type metadata, System One prompt templates, native score readouts and calibrated output formatting. Kev conversion merges alpha/r * B@A into floating-point base weights before later quantization, and embeds the pointer head in the GGUF. Inference weights are therefore adapted even though original matrices were fixed during LoRA training. Laya/Julia output option-marker scores; Kev outputs query/key vectors and dot products; lev/OpenJev read selected vocabulary logits. Causal tasks can share prompt prefixes. Multiple questions and lev's two choice variants can require multiple evaluations: zero output tokens is not one physical forward operation per HTTP request. This endpoint is for inference and does not supply a CLM training pipeline.
Sources: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29818 ; https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/conversion/lev.py ; https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/server-decision.cpp .

slides.title: How SGLang scores decisions
slides.body:
/v1/decisions and /v1/systemone are merged
Chat-model label logits; no generated tokens
One prompt per question; normal prefix caching
Checked: Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
Native Intern-Decision support is an open PR
slides.footer: Vocabulary scoring differs from Kev and CLM heads
slides.notes:
Status checked October 2, 2026. The shipped generic API requires no new decision head: chat-template prompts with thinking disabled score single-token answer labels via the shared /v1/score path. PR #41208 merged September 25; the earlier #40992 was closed into that stack. One prompt is built per question and items are batched. The generation/scoring request uses max_new_tokens=0. Ordinary Radix caching reuses token prefixes rather than separately encoded actions. Benefit: reuse a served chat model with no head training. Costs: each new state/question still needs prompt encoding and prefill, and the documentation's validated models are large. Models named on slide were validated on one H200 in BF16; this is not proof of free-GPU fit or a head-to-head latency benchmark. Label softmax is conditional on offered labels; label_mass/x_label_mass exposes full-vocabulary mass, and confidence needs task calibration. Hybrid-attention probabilities may shift across cold/warm cache and batch composition. LoRA adapter selection through the request is refused. Native Intern-Decision 0.8B/2B/4B option-marker support in #41712 (2B unverified; prerequisite #41724), and generic image input in #41922, are open proposals, not merged capabilities. Native Kev pointer-head and CLM projection-head support is not established by these docs.
Sources: https://lmsysorg.mintlify.app/docs/supported-models/decision_models ; https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41208 ; https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41712 ; https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41724 ; https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41922 .

slides.title: A fair Kev-versus-CLM comparison
slides.body:
Use the same boards, labels and legal actions
Time cold and warm caches on one device
Measure accuracy, captures, dots and latency
Record training time and peak memory
Match backbones to isolate the architecture
slides.footer: Released-model comparisons also include size and data effects
slides.notes:
A product comparison can compare actual released checkpoints, but its result combines backbone size, pretraining, decision data, objective, head and runtime. An architecture experiment should match the pretrained backbone, input budget, examples, splits, training budget and hardware, and vary joint pointer/LoRA versus frozen dual-encoder heads deliberately. Include a rule-based teacher baseline. Record encoder time separately from projection/scoring and end-to-end latency; use p50/p95 over enough repeats, cache-cold and action-cache-warm runs, identical quantization where meaningful, peak allocated memory, hardware model and checkpoint IDs. A smaller Kev may cost less at inference despite CLM's reusable actions. This is a proposed protocol, not measured results.

slides.title: Our Kev-4B Pac-Man lab
slides.body:
Train Pac-Man with fixed-code ghosts
Start from Qwen3.5-4B-Base
Train fresh LoRA and a pointer head
Complete four general stages before class
Fine-tune your own checkpoint for moves
slides.footer: Published Kev base recipe, followed by our Pac-Man adaptation
slides.notes: The main lab uses Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B-Base@1001bb4d826a52d1f399e183466143f4da7b741b, fresh rank-16 LoRA (alpha 32) targeting all projections and a 256-dimensional pointer head. Follow the four general training stages in Kev-4B's released curriculum, each in a separate notebook cell and checkpoint. Stage 5 warm-starts the learner's skills checkpoint for Pac-Man imitation. The original base matrices remain fixed while LoRA changes effective features. Calibration is separate and is not fitted or copied from the release. A 0.8B adapter cannot initialize the 4B model. Sources: https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b ; https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/84847f0a883d900f7de5b7a57eaa341ca7f9a6b4/experiments/q35-4b-s23.json

slides.title: Our 90-minute route
slides.body:
0-10    Compare architectures and play
10-20  Inspect the four general training stages
20-30  Review Pac-Man player labels
30-60  Fine-tune LoRA and the pointer head
60-80  Compare cost and player decisions
80-90  Explain and submit
slides.footer: Four general stages are prework. Fine-tuning takes 30 class minutes.
slides.notes: Installation, optimized-kernel verification, downloads and all four general decision stages are prework. Keep 90 minutes in class with a mandatory 30-minute Pac-Man fine-tuning block: inspect for 5 minutes, train within a 20-minute attempt cap, inspect/save for 5 minutes. These are scheduling budgets, not measured training durations. Check the separate initial, dates, documents and skills configurations and TensorBoard curves. Source: https://github.com/yxc20089/QPlusLearning/tree/main/labs/lab-01-kev-pacman

slides.title: Colab runtime for this lab
slides.body:
Target: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 96 GB
PyTorch 2.8 / CUDA 12.8 with BF16
Required: FLA and CUDA causal convolution
Verify Kev loss and backward before training
Use checkpointing and fused AdamW
slides.footer: Colab GPU availability varies. The target is not a free-compute promise.
slides.notes: Kev-4B retains a hybrid Gated DeltaNet/full-attention backbone. Install hash-pinned flash-linear-attention/fla-core 0.5.2, causal-conv1d 1.7.0 (cp313, Torch 2.8, CUDA 12, Linux x86_64 CXX11 ABI), einops 0.8.1 and Ninja 1.13.0 without replacing Kev's frozen Torch 2.8.0/CUDA 12.8, Triton 3.4.0, Transformers 5.17.0 and PEFT stack. Require BF16 and verify actual loss/backward/LoRA-head gradients plus fused AdamW on two suite records. Reference-kernel fallback fails the check. This checks compatibility rather than full-stage memory or timing. Default execution: batch 1 × accumulation 8, non-reentrant checkpointing, row_budget 2048; full attention uses SDPA. Inference-only Kev fusion/CUDA graphs remain disabled for training. The course has no completed GPU run of this 4B setup. Colab allocation varies, including on paid plans; arrange access and measure compute-unit cost. T4/P100 do not satisfy this optimized training contract. Sources: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/qwen3_5 ; https://github.com/fla-org/flash-linear-attention/releases/tag/v0.5.2 ; https://github.com/Dao-AILab/causal-conv1d/releases/tag/v1.7.0 ; https://research.google.com/colaboratory/faq.html

slides.title: CP1: score a legal player move
slides.body:
Pack state, question and legal options
Read decision-token and option-token features
Score each option with the pointer head
Read probabilities by direction name
Apply the move through the game code
slides.footer: The model chooses Pac-Man's move. Game code advances the ghosts.
slides.notes:
The game constructs caller-supplied criteria containing legal directions and their destination tiles. Kev jointly encodes state, question and options. Its head has query/key Linear projections from hidden_size to 256 and computes scaled dot products, then softmax over options. Hybrid Qwen3.5 handles each question as a causal row continuing from the shared state. This is contextual option scoring, unlike CLM's independent action encodings. Legal directions come from the maze rules. Probability reflects the offered options and is not a maze-clearing probability. The notebook serves the learner's initial checkpoint through /v1/systemone and connects the game via a Colab callback.
Sources: pinned Kev model.py PointerHead, rows_of and encode; lab/pacman_lab.py.

slides.title: What a probability tells us
slides.body:
Select the highest-scoring legal action
Inspect competing directions
Compare calibration on labelled examples
Confidence is not maze success
A legal move can still be strategically poor
slides.footer: Use the same actions and calibration protocol when comparing models
slides.notes:
Temperature and confidence formulas differ across wrappers, even behind System One-compatible APIs. Fit or evaluate calibration on development data, preserve it for evaluation, and compare Brier or log loss rather than assuming one shared confidence cutoff is meaningful. A one-step teacher label is not a full-game reward target. Keep learner uncertainty discussion tied to observed paired decisions, not a guarantee of safety or optimal play.
Sources: pinned Kev api.py; pinned CLM schema.py; llama.cpp tools/server/server-decision.cpp.

slides.title: Kev-4B training stages
slides.body:
1  Decisions: 12,576 records × 2 epochs
2  Dates/evidence: 1,425 + 2,000 replay
3  Documents: 5,219 + 2,000 replay
4  Skills/devtools: 11,320 + 4,000 replay
5  Pac-Man: 64 labelled boards × 2 epochs
slides.footer: Stages 1–4 are prework. Stage 5 is the mandatory class adaptation.
slides.notes: Stage 1 selects seed 2 in experiments/q35-4b-s23.json: 12,576 source records, two epochs, lr 5e-5, batch 4 × accumulation 2, checkpointing, BF16 autocast over FP32 parameters, rank 16/alpha 32, head 256; no init_from. Stage 2: dates/missing evidence, 1,425 new + 2,000 replay, one epoch, lr 2e-5, batch 4 × accumulation 2, seed 1. Stage 3: documents-v1 train, 5,219 new + 2,000 replay, one epoch, lr 2e-5, batch 2 × accumulation 4, max_state 7552, seed 2. Stage 4: hard-v1 train (6,000) + devtools-v1 train (5,320) with 4,000 replay, one epoch, lr 2e-5, batch 2 × accumulation 4, max_state 7552, seed 1. Expected steps: 3144, 429, 903, 1915. All general stages preserve option/none/distractor augmentation and p_none_pair=.25. Default lab execution uses batch 1 × accumulation 8, checkpointing and row_budget 2048: same effective batch/curriculum/schedule, different grouping/dropout and kernel numerics. The skills concatenation uses verified public partitions and a course checksum; byte identity to the historical round10 joint file is not asserted. Replay uses decision-v7 train only. General attempt caps are configurable 180 minutes, not predictions. Stage 5: 64 Pac-Man train boards, two epochs, lr 2e-5, batch 1 × accumulation 8, 16 steps, no none/distractor insertion, retained option shuffling. All five output directories and backups remain separate. Sources: https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/84847f0a883d900f7de5b7a57eaa341ca7f9a6b4/experiments/q35-4b-s23.json ; https://github.com/jaredpalmer/kev/blob/84847f0a883d900f7de5b7a57eaa341ca7f9a6b4/experiments/night2-4b-du.json ; https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b/blob/957b91e762e883935830246eeb02381f9d2694b6/training_config.json ; https://huggingface.co/jaredpalmer/kev-4b/blob/6cfce5c2fa4b4bd64026336ab649c5ca78857d52/training_config.json

slides.title: CP3: 30 minutes of fine-tuning
slides.body:
5 min    Inspect labelled moves and the loss
20 min  Fine-tune your skills checkpoint
5 min    Inspect and save the adapter/head
Update LoRA and the pointer head together
Keep original base matrices unchanged
slides.footer: Mandatory domain adaptation, warm-started with --init_from
slides.notes: Warm-start the learner's Stage 4 skills/devtools checkpoint with init_from, then use reviewed Pac-Man training JSONL. Two epochs, lr 2e-5, batch 1 × accumulation 8, BF16 autocast over FP32 weights, gradient checkpointing, state budget 2048. Sixty-four accepted rows give 16 steps. Disable none/distractor augmentation to retain legal directions; option shuffling remains active. Stop inference before training and reload afterward. The 20-minute training cap is a class budget pending a full GPU run. After interruption, use RESUME_PACMAN with the same inputs/arguments and an existing recovery snapshot, or explicitly label an instructor checkpoint. Source: pinned Kev README custom-data training and course cloud_runtime.py.

slides.title: Check what training changed
slides.body:
Trainable: LoRA and pointer-head parameters
Original base matrices remain fixed
Encoder features change through LoRA
Track loss and live memory in TensorBoard
Save recovery weights during every stage
slides.footer: Fixed base matrices still allow gradients through the encoder
slides.notes: Audit LoRA A/B and head as the only trainable parameters. Original matrices stay fixed while gradients pass through the encoder. Every optimizer step logs CE, learning rate, gradients, duration and peak/live allocated/reserved/free VRAM to TensorBoard/JSONL/CSV. Per-forward row counts/token shapes and record IDs remain in batches.jsonl. Save LoRA/head plus optimizer/scheduler/RNG/counters after step 1, every 100 steps or five minutes at optimizer boundaries, and the final step. Keep the latest two complete recovery snapshots. Native Kev resume is full-weight-only; the lab supplies guarded LoRA continuation. Use Drive storage or export snapshots before Colab disconnects. The older 0.8B notebook saved weights only at completion, so its failed step-2073 run had no automatic learned checkpoint. Source: course training_monitor.py and lora_recovery.py.

slides.title: CP4: compare the same boards
slides.body:
Fix skills and Pac-Man checkpoints
Score the same 16 evaluation boards
Compare teacher accuracy and captures
Save paired predictions by board ID
Include a deterministic rules baseline
slides.footer: One maze and 16 boards do not establish general game skill
slides.notes: Compare the learner's completed Stage 4 general checkpoint and Stage 5 Pac-Man checkpoint. Keep backbone, legal actions, ghost rules and precision fixed. Freeze the candidate before viewing evaluation. Report heuristic teacher agreement, immediate captures, unchanged decisions and regressions. The release's scores and calibration do not transfer to these runs. Source: course pacman_lab.py.

slides.title: CP4: compare cost and gameplay
slides.body:
Use identical starts and fixed-code ghosts
Compare dots collected and game turns
Measure end-to-end decision latency
Record actual training time and peak memory
Record Colab compute units consumed
slides.footer: Gameplay quality and inference speed are separate outcomes
slides.notes:
Keep the existing capped 24-turn initial/fine-tuned rollout pair and rules teacher. Two trajectories illustrate behavior, not average win rate. Save HTTP latency for paired evaluations and report enough repeats for a meaningful later p50/p95 benchmark. CUDA kernel/graph options and serving precision affect latency. Keep them identical and state this notebook disables optional fused kernels/graphs for its reference path. Record upstream peak_device_bytes and training wall_seconds, helper elapsed time including load/save, and actual Colab compute-unit use rather than inventing a fixed dollar rate. No GPU or live browser results have been collected for this revision. Broader evaluation needs multiple starts and held-out mazes.

slides.title: The community starting point
slides.body:
Source: codaaiteam/jev-pacman, MIT
Original demo: human player, Jev ghosts
Our design: learned player, fixed-code ghosts
Use the same maze and rules for every model
No ROM setup for this browser clone
slides.footer: Clean upstream source and MIT notice are preserved
slides.notes:
This is an adaptation of the independently authored MIT Jev Pac-Man game, not an official Kev/CLM game release. Preserve the maze, renderer and license. Replace controllers so the learned model controls Pac-Man and fixed code controls ghosts. The notebook integrates the player's /v1/systemone request with a Colab callback and provides Python evaluation/rollouts. GPU training and live callback need instructor preflight. The comparison/lab slides are native editable objects. The original 30-slide lecture stays unchanged.
